behavior_items: The bug report describes an optimization-dependent false positive from GCC's -Warray-bounds warning, specifically triggered at -O2 when a pointer returned from an inline array-access helper is later used in a memset on a non-leading struct field.

The intended source logic is: an inline function checks whether an index is within bounds of an array of structures; if the index is valid it returns a pointer to the selected element, otherwise it returns NULL.

A caller then passes the returned pointer to a reset-style function that writes to one of the structure's members using memset. Semantically, this write is only valid on the non-NULL path, because NULL represents the out-of-range case.

The reproducer's important control-flow property is that the chosen index is known to be valid in the real program logic; the bug report even notes the original code used a loop such as idx < ary->objcnt, so the NULL-returning branch is provably unreachable for those iterations.

Despite that, after inlining and optimization at -O2, GCC emits a warning on memset(&obj->field1, 0xff, sizeof(obj->field1)) claiming the accessed range is out of bounds [0, 0]. That wording is characteristic of GCC reasoning as if the base object had size 0, which commonly corresponds to treating the base pointer as possibly or definitely NULL.

The warning only appearing at -O2 and not at -O0/-O1 shows the behavior depends on later optimization/value-range analysis rather than simple front-end parsing. In other words, the diagnostic is produced after transformations that change GCC's internal understanding of the pointer.

The report suggests GCC incorrectly concludes that obj must be NULL, or at least propagates a null-based object size into the warning machinery on a path that should represent the valid in-bounds element.

The specific expression memset(&obj->field1, ...) is important: taking the address of a member at a nonzero offset from obj makes a NULL interpretation visible to the bounds checker. If obj were NULL, &obj->field1 would denote an address derived from offsetting from a zero-sized/null base, which matches the reported 'offset [0, 7] out of bounds [0, 0]' style.

The note that the memset target cannot be the first field in the struct is a key reproducer condition. If the field were at offset 0, GCC's internal representation of the access may not trigger the same offset-from-NULL bounds logic, so the false positive disappears or changes form.

This means the reproducer is exercising not just general nullness analysis, but the interaction between struct-member offset computation, object-size/bounds inference, and built-in memset diagnostics after optimization.

Because the helper is inline and defined in a header-style pattern, GCC can fold the array lookup, propagate constants, and merge control-flow facts across caller and callee. That aggressive simplification is likely necessary to expose the mistaken internal state that later feeds the warning.

The underlying array lookup pattern likely resembles returning &array[idx] when idx is within count and NULL otherwise. This is a common safe idiom, so the reproducer is valuable because it shows GCC warning on ordinary defensive code rather than on actual out-of-bounds behavior.

The diagnostic points at memset rather than the array access itself because GCC's array-bounds/object-size checker is attached to built-in memory functions. Once it believes the destination object has size 0, the memset range check reports the member-sized write as exceeding the available bounds.

The workaround mentioned in the report—writing some structure field before the memset—suggests that introducing an additional observable dereference helps GCC reestablish that obj is non-NULL on the reachable path. That further supports the idea that the warning stems from an internal path-sensitivity or propagation bug, not from the source semantics.

Overall, the reproducer exercises a false-positive compiler diagnostic path where valid array index reasoning and non-NULL object use are lost or corrupted during -O2 optimization, causing GCC to misdiagnose a member memset as an out-of-bounds access from a zero-sized/null base object.

This routine is called to check builtin_unreachable calls during any time before final removal. The only way we can be sure it does not provide any additional information is to expect that we can update the global values of all exports from a block. This means the branch to the unreachable call must dominate all uses of those ssa-names, with the exception that there can be a single use in the block containing the branch. IF the name used in the branch is defined in the block, it may contain the name of something else that will be an export. And likewise that may also use another name that is an export etc. As long as there is only a single use, we can be sure that there are no other side effects (like being passed to a call, or stored to a global, etc. This means we will miss cases where there are 2 or more uses that have no interveneing statements that may had side effects, but it catches most of the caes we care about, and prevents expensive in depth analysis. Ranger will still reflect the proper ranges at other places in these missed cases, we simply will not remove/set globals early.
